body: Hironobu Sakaguchi (坂口 博信, Sakaguchi Hironobu; born November 25, 1962) is a Japanese game designer, director, producer, and writer. Originally working for Square (later Square Enix) from 1983 to 2003, he departed the company and founded independent studio Mistwalker in 2004. He is known as the creator of the Final Fantasy franchise, in addition to other titles during his time at Square. At Mistwalker, he is known for creating the Blue Dragon and Terra Battle series among several standalone titles like Lost Odyssey, as well as later moving away from home consoles and creating titles for mobile platforms.

Final Fantasy from 1987 is the project that permanently links Sakaguchi's name to Square's history. The game is born inside a company still far smaller than the one the series would help build, and combines a staged journey with turn-based battles, classes, towns and a world that gradually opens up. The historical point does not lie in the myth of the "final game" told as an individual legend, but in a team's ability to transform references from computer role-playing games into a structure suited to Famicom. Sakaguchi plays a central role in the project's direction and organization, alongside figures such as Nobuo Uematsu and Yoshitaka Amano. A production model emerges in which systems, music and visual identity are perceived as coordinated parts of the same journey.

With Final Fantasy's success, Sakaguchi gradually moves from direct direction to supervision and production of increasingly large projects. This transformation is important for understanding his career: the author is not a person who controls every detail, but someone who builds conditions in which different specialists can work toward the same direction. Later entries in the series bring forward new directors, artists, programmers and writers, while Sakaguchi assumes broader production responsibilities. His contribution changes form along with the scale of the Japanese industry. Distinguishing these roles avoids attributing to him individually decisions made by complex teams, but also helps explain his organizational influence. Square's growth in the 1990s is a story of technology and markets, but also of delegation, trust and creative coordination.

Final Fantasy VII shows how much Sakaguchi's role has changed since the early days. On the 1997 project he is producer, while direction is entrusted to Yoshinori Kitase. The distinction is essential because the transition to 3D, pre-rendered backgrounds and CD-ROM distribution comes from the work of a much larger organization. Sakaguchi helps support this production transformation and a narrative vision capable of reaching an international audience, but he should not be treated as the sole author of every choice. The game also becomes a turning point for Square's economic and technical scale, with computer-generated scenes and an amount of content difficult to imagine on cartridge. His career therefore also tells the evolution of video-game authorship: from hands-on director to producer of large creative systems.

After leaving Square, Sakaguchi founds Mistwalker in 2004 and rebuilds his work around a leaner structure, often collaborating with outside studios for technical production. Blue Dragon and Lost Odyssey show this phase: large role-playing games for Xbox 360 created through networks of collaborators, with the return of historical figures such as Nobuo Uematsu and new partners for graphics and development. The choice lets Sakaguchi focus more on concept, scenario and overall direction without recreating internally a company the size of the old Square. It is a different production model, suited to a creator who wants to keep making ambitious worlds without an enormous corporate structure. Mistwalker therefore becomes not only a new label, but an experiment in how to organize creation after a long industrial career.

The Last Story, released on Wii, shows Sakaguchi willing to question conventions of the role-playing game that he had helped consolidate. Combat works in real time, uses cover, positioning and abilities that can change the space, while the party remains the emotional center of the adventure. This combination shifts attention from abstract command selection to immediate reading of the field. For Sakaguchi, it is also a more direct return to directing a project after years focused mainly on production. The title demonstrates that his authorial identity is not synonymous with turn-based combat. What remains recognizable instead is his interest in a group of characters forced to build trust during a journey, while the game rules make that collaboration physically perceptible.

Fantasian uses photographs of physical dioramas to create its environments. Not counting smaller variations, over 150 dioramas were created by ten companies across Japan. Several of the modellers had never worked on a video game project before, encountering some difficulties creating objects and environments from the illustrations provided. Diorama modeller Tomohiro Yatsubo remembered them modeling their environment "down to the millimeter" to properly reflect Sakaguchi's plan. The Quail airship was created by Marbling Fine Arts's Hiroshi Ihara based on the concept of "a boat with beautiful curves". LED lights were used in the models as light sources, such as interior lights and fires in the Quail. A notable contributor was Akira Toriyama, with whom Sakaguchi had worked on a number of projects, who submitted a diorama under a pseudonym. As the dioramas took shape, Sakaguchi used them to inform his work on the game's design.

original.old_body: Hironobu Sakaguchi is born on November 25, 1962, a Japanese creator and producer whose name is decisively linked to the birth of Final Fantasy. His career crosses very different phases: the Square years, the international growth of Japanese role-playing games, the cinematic experiment of The Spirits Within, his departure from the company and the founding of Mistwalker. Reducing him to a single franchise, however, hides a more interesting continuity. His projects repeatedly return to teamwork, the close relationship with music and visual imagination, and the desire to build worlds in which travel is also a sequence of relationships. From Final Fantasy to Lost Odyssey, The Last Story and Fantasian, Sakaguchi changes technology and production scale, but continues to treat the video game as a collective work that lives in the meeting of systems, images and memory.

original.old_body: Fantasian brings Sakaguchi back to a different production scale and makes his interest in the relationship between craft and technology visible. Environments are built as physical dioramas, photographed and integrated with three-dimensional characters. The choice produces imperfect surfaces, real materials and a visual depth difficult to obtain by simply imitating miniature sets in computer graphics. In the interview published on the App Store, Sakaguchi also connects the project to his personal history with video games and his long collaboration with Nobuo Uematsu. Fantasian therefore does not try to recreate the past literally: it uses contemporary tools to recover the pleasure of building a world by hand. After decades of increasingly digital production, the diorama becomes a new narrative technology because it makes the material presence behind the image perceptible.

context_paragraphs: The characters were designed by Takatoshi Goto. Sakaguchi described Goto's designs as doing a good job expression the multiple worlds featured, noting that each lead was given a key color and tied into the story themes. The in-game character models were designed to fit in with the diorama environments, having realistic proportions and a soft doll-like texture. Character animations were done by hand to reinforce this style. The concept art and Memory illustrations were created by Manabu Kusunoki, who had worked with Sakaguchi on multiple projects. Ikeda described working with real-world dioramas as a refreshing change from his usual design work. During pre-production, concept dioramas were created by Walnuts Claywork Studio's Tomohiro Yatsubo, who had worked on similar environments for Terra Wars. A Terra Wars diorama kept in the studio was used for early testing. Due to the design approach, environments were fixed early on, as any changes such as new roads or zone exits would need a lot of work. Due to limitations with camera size and angles, some environment redesigns were needed. Nishikawa was in charge of coordinating the dioramas. The original plan to 3D scan the dioramas into the game proved unworkable, with Nakamura creating an alternate method of extracting 3D information from photographs, with flat environments being more difficult to scan in.

editorial_features.title: Choosing a story from many hands
editorial_features.summary: A world built from shared contributions.
body: Tetsuya Nomura remembered Final Fantasy VI as a small workplace where a job title did not confine an idea. Staff submitted story proposals for Sakaguchi and other senior colleagues to select. Nomura's work concerned monsters and battle visuals, yet a document he wrote with another employee helped establish machinery alongside magic. Its ideas included the Magitek walkers in the snow. The producer's decision was therefore a point of selection within a conversation, rather than evidence that the entire world originated with him.

Shadow makes that shared process visible. Nomura contributed the character's broad outline, his accompanying dog and an inn scene. He also insisted that colleagues added other elements. Director Yoshinori Kitase made the decision that failing to wait during the Floating Continent's destruction could lose Shadow permanently. Different kinds of authorship met inside one character: an artist's proposal, subsequent additions and a director's rule for the player's actions. Naming only the series creator would conceal the particular decisions that gave this relationship its shape.

editorial_features.title: Learning what a producer carries
editorial_features.summary: A world built from shared contributions.
body: Tetsuya Takahashi later described leaving the Final Fantasy team during VII to attempt worlds built throughout in three dimensions. Leading that separate group exposed work he had previously seen Sakaguchi carry: helping inexperienced colleagues adjust, discussing their anxieties and holding a project together while its methods were unsettled. This recollection shifts attention away from a producer's public title. The technical ambition also created a human problem, because the team had to learn its tools while learning how to work with one another.

editorial_features.title: Leaving room for another imagination
editorial_features.summary: A world built from shared contributions.
body: In the same conversation, Sakaguchi described returning to everyday direction on The Last Story. He also acknowledged a limit: he could not draw the world he wanted. Specialists needed freedom to make it richer than his own visual imagination. His account connects involvement with delegation, rather than treating them as opposites. It remains a participant's account of leadership, not an independent judgment of workplace conditions. What it does reveal is the practical dependence of an apparently personal vision on other people's skills.

What it does reveal is the practical dependence of an apparently personal vision on other people's skills.

old_entry.title: Touch Me
old_entry.summary: Touch Me is an arcade game first released by Atari Inc. in 1974, and later as a handheld game in 1978.
body: Touch Me is an arcade game first released by Atari Inc. in 1974, and later as a handheld game in 1978. It can be described as a Simon  Says-like game that involves touching a series of buttons that light up and produce sounds. The player must observe a sequence of blinking electric lights and repeat the sequence back in the same order that it occurred. Each time this is completed, the game will produce another sequence with an additional button added. This process is repeated and a digital score window displays the total number of sound sequences a player correctly repeats. The game continues until the maximum sequence of buttons is reached, or the user makes a mistake.

Touch Me was first released as an arcade game in 1974 by Atari. The arcade version was housed in a short arcade cabinet and had four large circular buttons of the same color. The player was allowed to make three mistakes before the game ended. The arcade game found itself competing for attention in arcades with the latest pinball machines and video games of the day; it was not very successful.

In 1977, Ralph Baer saw potential in the "Simon Says" concept behind the Touch Me game. He copied Atari's game, adding colored buttons and musical sound effects, and created the Simon handheld game, which became a major success.
Seeing this, Atari sought to capitalize on the success of Simon and released their own handheld version of Touch Me in 1978.
An emulated handheld version of Touch Me was included in the 2022 compilation Atari 50.

old_entry.title: Santa Paravia en Fiumaccio
old_entry.summary: Santa Paravia en Fiumaccio is a video game in which each player becomes the ruler of a fledgling Italian city-state around the year 1400.
body: Santa Paravia en Fiumaccio is a video game in which each player becomes the ruler of a fledgling Italian city-state around the year 1400. The goal of the game is to become king or queen; to do so the player must manage their city-state so that it may grow.

The game, by George Blank, first appeared in the December 1978 issue of  SoftSide magazine, (Milford, NH), and was published for sale on tape cassette as a computer game by Instant Software (Peterborough, NH) for the Radio Shack TRS-80, Apple II, TI-99/4A, and Commodore PET. It has been translated into many languages, such as ANSI C, and has been ported to the Palm`Pilot.

Santa Paravia is a kingdom‑management game in which the player advances through ranks of royalty by overseeing land, grain, population, and treasury; each turn the player buys or sells grain and land, releases grain to peasants to influence population and starvation, and sets customs, income tax, tariffs, and justice. Seasonal sowing and harvest depend on grain reserves, weather, and rats, while income allows the player to purchase marketplaces, mills, palaces, cathedrals, and soldiers. As the realm grows, merchants, clergy, nobles, and higher status appear, but mills and merchants require peasants to operate, and all economic and social factors interact in complex, irreversible ways.
All Game Guide called Santa Paravia and Fiumaccio an enjoyable and entertaining strategy game. Moves liked the graphic dsplay in Santa Paravia en Fiumaccio.

old_entry.title: The Cottage
old_entry.summary: The Cottage (Swedish: Stugan) is an adventure video game that was initially made available in 1978 for the DEC-10 mainframe computer Oden in Stockholm, and later published by Scandinavian PC Systems for IBM PCs in 1986 in Swedish, Danish, Norwegian and English.
body: The Cottage (Swedish: Stugan) is an adventure video game that was initially made available in 1978 for the DEC-10 mainframe computer Oden in Stockholm, and later published by Scandinavian PC Systems for IBM PCs in 1986 in Swedish, Danish, Norwegian and English. It was the first publicly available Swedish adventure game and one of the first commercial Swedish video games.

The game is set in a cottage in Småland, Sweden; the player explores the cottage and its surroundings by typing simple commands to indicate what they want to do or where they want to go. They aim to find items and perform certain actions to raise their score and rank, while avoiding traps and enemy characters, with the ultimate goal of getting inducted into the cottage council.

The game was developed in the 1970s and 1980s by Viggo Kann, Kimmo Eriksson and Olle Johansson, three children who had played the game Adventure and wanted to create a similar game in Swedish. The Cottage began as a collection of smaller games the three had previously developed on their own, with the player moving through an amusement arcade to choose what to play; as they found it more fun to move through the arcade than to play the games, they ended up expanding the area to explore and removing most of the smaller games. Several thousand copies of the IBM PC release were sold; despite this, the developers did not receive much money from it outside of pre-paid royalties. The game had a cult-like status among Oden users at the time, and was commercially important to the computer center in Stockholm.

old_entry.title: Bosconian
old_entry.summary: Bosconian is a 1981 multidirectional shooter video game developed and published by Namco for arcades.
body: Bosconian is a 1981 multidirectional shooter video game developed and published by Namco for arcades. It was released by Midway Manufacturing in North America. The goal is to earn as many points as possible by destroying enemy missiles and bases using a ship which shoots simultaneously both the front and back.

Bosconian was commercially successful in Japan and received positive critical reception, but did not achieve the global commercial success of other shoot 'em ups from the golden age of arcade video games. It was ported to home computers as Bosconian '87 (1987) and spawned two sequels: Blast Off (1989) and Final Blaster (1990). Since its release, Bosconian has been regarded by critics as influential in the shoot 'em up genre.

old_entry.title: Xevious
old_entry.summary: Xevious is a 1983 vertically scrolling shooter video game developed and published by Namco for arcades.
body: Xevious is a 1983 vertically scrolling shooter video game developed and published by Namco for arcades. It was released in Japan and in North America by Atari, Inc. in February 1983. Controlling the Solvalou starship, the player attacks Xevious forces before they destroy all of mankind. The Solvalou has two weapons at its disposal: a zapper to destroy flying craft, and a blaster to bomb ground installations and enemies. It runs on the Namco Galaga arcade system. An upgraded version, Super Xevious, was released in December 1984.

The game was designed by Masanobu Endō and a small team. Created to rival the success of Scramble, it was originally themed around the Vietnam War and titled Cheyenne. Endō wanted the game to have a detailed, integral storyline and a comprehensive world, and to be welcoming for newer players. Several enemies and characters were made to pay homage to other popular science fiction works, including Star Wars, UFO, Alien and Battlestar Galactica.

Xevious was praised for its detailed graphics, challenge and originality. It became an unprecedented success for Namco in Japan, with record-breaking sales figures making it the biggest game since Space Invaders. The North American release paled in comparison, despite still selling 5,295 arcade units by the end of 1983. It has been listed among the most influential games in the shoot 'em up genre, establishing the template for vertically scrolling shooters and inspiring games such as TwinBee and RayForce. It was ported to home systems, followed by several sequels and spin-offs, and is included in many Namco compilations.

old_entry.title: Dog Star Adventure
old_entry.summary: Dog Star Adventure is a text adventure game written by Lance Micklus in TRS-80 BASIC and published as the cover article in the May 1979 issue of SoftSide magazine.
body: Dog Star Adventure is a text adventure game written by Lance Micklus in TRS-80 BASIC and published as the cover article in the May 1979 issue of SoftSide magazine. It is historically notable as the first example of the source code to a text adventure being published, and as a result, many later text adventures are based on its concepts.

The game takes place in the Star Wars universe, loosely following the plot of the movie during the action that takes place on the Death Star. Names of the various characters are changed to avoid copyright issues. The player has to gather a number of items to repair their ship, rescue princess Leya, and escape without being detected by the many Roche Soldiers.

old_entry.title: Head On
old_entry.summary: Head On is an arcade video game developed by Sega/Gremlin and released by Sega in 1979.
body: Head On is an arcade video game developed by Sega/Gremlin and released by Sega in 1979. It was the first maze video game where the goal is to run over dots. Designed by Lane Hauck at Sega/Gremlin in the United States, it was the fourth highest-grossing arcade game of 1979 in both Japan and the US.
Sega released a sequel, Head On Part II, later the same year. The original inspired a number of clones, as well as Namco's Rally-X (1980).

Two cars continuously drive forward through rectangular channels in a simple maze. At the four cardinal directions are gaps where a car can change lanes. The player goal is to collect all dots in the maze while avoiding collisions with the computer-controlled car that is travelling in the opposite direction.

The game was developed by Sega/Gremlin in the United States, designed by Lane Hauck. He brainstormed the concept in 1978, roughly around the time that Sega purchased Gremlin Industries. After the acquisition, veteran Sega engineer Shikanosuke Ochi had a look at a prototype of Head On and suggested a change. Originally, the rounds in Head On were dictated by a timer as most games of the 1970s were, but Taito's Space Invaders introduced the concept of lives. Ochi suggested to Hauck that he should get rid of the timer and replace it with a lives system, which Hauck implemented and later said was "key to making the game big".

The game has two different orientations for horizontal and vertical monitors. In Japan, the game was released with a vertical orientation to suit the cocktail table arcade cabinets popular in Japan. In the US, the game was displayed horizontally inside of a standard upright cabinet.

Head On was a commercial success in arcades. In Japan, it became Gremlin's most successful export and a highly influential game in the period after the Space Invaders boom. It was Japan's fourth highest-grossing arcade game of 1979, below Space Invaders, Galaxian and Sega's Monaco GP. Head On was also the fourth highest-earning arcade video game of 1979 in the United States, below Space Invaders, Football and Sprint 2.

Head On's relation to Pac-Man (1980) as a game about collecting dots inside of a maze-like structure has been noted by commentators and historians. Though there has not been direct confirmation on its influence, the importance of Head On in Japan around the time of Pac-Man's development suggests a correlation between the two. Several evolutions on the Head On formula released in 1979 including Space Chaser (1979) and Car Hunt (1979) bear further resemblance to Pac-Man.

Ports of Head On for the Commodore 64 and VIC-20 were released in 1982. In Japan, the game was released for the PC-8801 and Sharp MZ computers.  Head On later appeared in the Sega Saturn collection Sega Memorial Selection Vol.1 and in the PlayStation 2 collection Sega Ages Vol. 23.
